quickAnswer: Sudbury is a town of owner-occupied single-family houses: 86.4% are detached, 92.1% of households own, and the median owner-occupied value is $892,700. Few homes pre-date 1940, so most of the housing is mid-century or newer.
body: ## A town of one-acre lots and owner-occupied houses

Sudbury's housing reads almost like a single type. The Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) counts 5,559 detached single-family houses among 6,432 housing units, an 86.4% share that ranks 7th of the 50 towns we serve. Owners live in 5,821 of 6,323 occupied homes (92.1%), and only 502 households rent. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $892,700, 9th-highest in the group.

Sudbury's history helps explain the pattern. Sudbury's 1-acre zoning bylaws helped keep a rural character through the 1970s and 1980s, when developments of single-family Colonials and large Capes made the town an affluent location. Large houses can mean long duct runs and several heating zones, which is where good sizing pays.
## Very few old houses, and a big middle

Only 401 homes (6.2%) date from 1939 or earlier, which is 48th of 50 towns. The weight sits in the middle decades: 1,298 homes (20.2%) from 1940 to 1959 and 1,910 (29.7%) from 1960 to 1979. Another 1,450 (22.5%) went up between 1980 and 1999, and 1,373 (21.3%) since 2000. The median year is 1975.

That middle group is the one to watch. Houses from the postwar decades through the 1970s can carry older insulation standards, original ductwork and later additions. Equipment sized for the original shell may not match the house as it stands today.
## Gas first, then oil and tank gas

Utility gas heats 3,924 occupied homes (62.1%), 9th highest in the group. Fuel oil or kerosene heats 1,671 (26.4%), and bottled or tank gas heats 302 (4.8%). Electricity heats just 407 homes (6.4%), 45th of 50.

Look at that last number. Few Sudbury households heat with electricity, so for most households a switch to a heat pump would be a change of fuel. For the 1,671 oil homes and the 302 on tank gas, a heat pump trades deliveries for a utility bill.
## What the town's history says about buildings

Incorporated in 1639, Sudbury once covered what is now Wayland and parts of Framingham, Marlborough, Stow and Maynard. The Sudbury Center Historic District has changed little since a new Town House went up in 1846, apart from the Town Hall, built in 1932 to replace the Town House that burned in 1930. The Wayside Inn, which claims to be the country's oldest operating inn, belongs to the same story. Historic buildings like these can be poor candidates for a standard installation. Old frames, plaster walls and little duct space may call for ductless heads or carefully routed pipes.
## Rebates when the utility is not named

We do not name Sudbury's electric utility here, because the town's utility is not confirmed in our records. Rebates run through the utility that serves your address, and your electric bill will tell you who that is. If that is a Mass Save sponsor, a 2026 whole-home heat pump can earn up to $8,500, provided the house is weatherized. Read the [heat pump page](/cities/sudbury/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) for the conditions.

Sudbury's place on the map matters too. The highest point in town is on the north slope of Nobscot Hill, and significant tracts of open space, including much wetland, were preserved in the northern half of town and along the Hop Brook corridor. Houses near wetland can have damp cellars, so humidity control belongs in the conversation about any new system.

faq.q: Why does a large Sudbury house need a heating load assessment?
faq.a: Because size alone is misleading. A big house with good windows and added insulation may need less heat than its square footage suggests, while a drafty one may need more. With 86.4% of homes detached, we assess the load room by room before we quote.

faq.q: Is a heat pump worth considering if I heat with oil in Sudbury?
faq.a: It is worth a comparison. About 26.4% of Sudbury homes burn oil, and a cold-climate heat pump can replace or share that load. The answer depends on insulation, the existing distribution and rebate eligibility, which we check at the estimate.

faq.q: Which utility serves my Sudbury address?
faq.a: Check your electric bill. We have not confirmed a single utility for the town, so rebate rules depend on the company that serves your home. If it is a Mass Save sponsor, the standard rebates apply; confirm at masssave.com.

faq.q: How do Sudbury's housing ages compare with the middle MetroWest town?
faq.a: Close to typical, apart from very few old houses. Only 6.2% of homes date from 1939 or earlier (48th of 50, against a 16.6% median), 56.1% were built before 1980 (median 57.2%) and 9.4% since 2010 (median 8.4%). The median year is 1975 in both. We still size equipment from the actual house, not from the averages.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Most Sudbury homes heat with utility gas (62.1%) or oil (26.4%), in houses with a median build year of 1975. We size a new boiler or furnace from the house as it is today, including any additions.
body: ## Replacing heat in a large-lot town

In a town where 86.4% of homes are detached houses, a heating replacement is usually one furnace or boiler for one house. Detached houses often get additions over the years, and a boiler sized for the original shell may no longer match the building as it stands. We size from the house in front of us.
### Choosing the fuel

Gas is the leading fuel at 3,924 homes, so a new gas furnace or boiler is the usual like-for-like replacement. The 1,671 oil homes are choosing between a new oil unit, a gas conversion if a main reaches the property and a heat pump. Houses on tank gas, 302 in all, can look at heat pumps as well.
### Zones and long runs

- Large houses often need two or more zones so bedrooms and living areas can be set separately.
- Long duct runs lose heat and push air weakly, which is why a duct inspection belongs in a furnace replacement.
- Radiant floors and baseboard loops in additions may need their own controls.
- A cold corner is often a sign of a poorly balanced system, not an undersized one.
### The mid-century question

Houses built from 1940 through the 1970s are the biggest group in Sudbury. Houses of that era can have original ductwork and older insulation, so air sealing and duct repair can reduce the load the new equipment must meet. We tell you if a smaller unit would do the job once the house is tightened.
### Permits and inspection

Swapping a gas furnace or boiler means a permit and a final inspection. Only a licensed plumber or gas fitter can pull the gas permit, and the town's building department can explain local steps. Venting and gas piping are planned around that inspection.
### Repair or replace

A fault in one part of a fairly young unit is usually a repair. A cracked heat exchanger, repeated breakdowns or a system near the end of its life point to replacement. Sudbury ranks 9th of 50 for gas heat, at 62.1% of occupied homes against a 41.9% median, so gas furnaces and boilers make up most of the replacement work, while oil, at 26.4% and 34th of 50, sits below the 36.5% median.

faq.q: Will a bigger Sudbury house need a bigger boiler?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Insulation, windows and air leakage matter as much as square footage. A large house with tight construction can need less capacity than a smaller drafty one. With a median owner-occupied value of $892,700 and 5,559 detached houses in town, we calculate the heating load house by house before choosing capacity.

faq.q: Can I add a zone to an existing heating system?
faq.a: Often yes, with extra thermostats and valves or dampers. Whether it works depends on the existing equipment and piping, so we look at the system first. Zoning is a common question in larger houses, where bedrooms and living areas call for different settings.

faq.q: What do I do when the heat stops in the middle of the night?
faq.a: Call (508) 786-8755; emergency calls are taken around the clock, and a free written estimate comes before work starts. If you heat with oil, check the tank and the burner reset first. Oil heats 1,671 Sudbury homes, and an empty tank is a simple cause worth ruling out before a service call.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: With 86.4% of Sudbury homes detached and a median year built of 1975, cooling choices come down to central air or a multi-zone ductless system. The right choice depends on existing ducts and on the size of the house.
body: ## Cooling big houses on big lots

Sudbury has 5,559 detached houses, 465 attached homes and only 408 homes in multi-unit buildings (143 in three- or four-unit buildings, 265 in larger ones). Detached houses can often take central air, since a condenser needs outdoor space and the air handler needs a basement or attic. Larger ones can also mean cooling a big volume of air over two or three floors.
### Central or ductless

A house with decent ducts can often take a central system if airflow is balanced. In a two-story house, upstairs rooms often run hot because heat rises and ducts are undersized. A second zone with its own thermostat is a common fix. Houses without ducts, or additions that sit beyond the reach of the old system, suit ductless heads.
### Heat pumps as a cooling option

A heat pump does both jobs. For a house that needs new cooling and has an aging oil or propane heating system, replacing both with one heat pump system can be sensible. The [heat pump page](/cities/sudbury/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) lays out what rebates exist.
### Our first questions

- Which rooms are hardest to cool, and are they above a garage or under a roof?
- How old are the ducts and how well are they sealed?
- Is there room for the outdoor unit away from bedrooms?
- Does the panel have capacity?
### Humidity and oversizing

A big house tempts people to buy a big air conditioner. A unit that is too large reaches the thermostat setting fast and stops before it has dried the air. Sizing from the real load avoids that damp, clammy feel.
### Repair or replace
Small parts such as capacitors, contactors and fans are common repairs. A compressor failure on an old unit is the case that usually tips toward replacement, and the estimate lays out both options.
### Newer houses

Another 1,373 Sudbury homes date from 2000 on. Newer houses are more likely to have been built with central air in mind, so the question may be service, zoning or replacing an aging unit. The 605 built since 2010 rank 20th of 50 for that band (9.4%, against an 8.4% median).

faq.q: Why is the upstairs of my Sudbury house so much hotter?
faq.a: Heat rises, and upstairs ducts are often small or long. A second zone, better balancing or a ductless head upstairs usually helps. A technician should check airflow first. Sudbury is 86.4% detached houses, and multi-floor houses are where this complaint is most common.

faq.q: Can I cool just an addition?
faq.a: Yes. A single-zone ductless head is the usual way to cool an addition without altering the main system. Because many Sudbury houses are large detached ones, a single head or a short multi-head setup can add cooling to one wing while the rest of the house keeps its existing arrangement.

faq.q: Does a house from 1975 or earlier need new ducts for central air?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Sudbury's median year built is 1975, and 56.1% of homes pre-date 1980. Many older houses were built without central air, so ducts may be missing or sized for heating only. We inspect what exists, and a ductless or small-duct layout is an option where it is not practical to add ducts.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: Sudbury's electric utility is not confirmed in our records, so the rebate path depends on the utility serving your address. In town, 1,671 homes burn oil and 302 use tank gas, and those are the households with a fuel to swap.
body: ## Heat pump rebates in Sudbury

We have not confirmed which electric utility serves Sudbury, so check your bill. A Mass Save sponsor would put a 2026 whole-home heat pump rebate of up to $8,500 on the table, after the house is weatherized. The conditions are on our [main heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
### Where Sudbury's ages fall

The year 2000 is the line that matters for weatherization. Sudbury has 1,373 homes (21.3%) from 2000 on, including 605 since 2010. The rest date from 1999 or earlier: 401 from 1939 or before, 1,298 from 1940 to 1959, 1,910 from 1960 to 1979 and 1,450 from 1980 to 1999. For those houses, an energy assessment is the usual first step.
### Who benefits

Oil homes (1,671) and tank-gas homes (302) swap a delivered fuel for electricity. Gas homes, the largest group at 3,924, deserve a careful comparison before changing. Electric heat is rare here: 407 homes (6.4%), 45th of 50, against a 10.1% median, so a heat pump is a fuel change for most Sudbury households.
### Big houses, several heads

A large house may need a ducted system, several ductless heads or a mix. Rooms over garages and finished basements often do well with heads of their own. See the [cooling page](/cities/sudbury/air-conditioning-installation-repair) for the layout questions.
### Partial-home option
A partial-home setup keeps a boiler or furnace for the coldest days, and its rebate works differently from the whole-home one.
### Single-family scale

Sudbury covers 24.6 square miles, and 5,559 of its 6,432 housing units are detached houses. Most heat pump jobs here are therefore single-family houses, with a median owner-occupied value of $892,700 that ranks 9th of 50. Only 408 homes are in multi-unit buildings, which ranks 45th, so the apartment-style ductless job is the exception.

faq.q: How do I know whether the Mass Save rebate applies to my Sudbury house?
faq.a: Look at your electric bill to see who supplies power, then check masssave.com. If a municipal utility serves your street, a different rule applies: Mass Save usually covers only homes heated with natural gas from a sponsor, and the municipal utility runs its own program for the rest. We can help work through eligibility at the estimate.

faq.q: Can a heat pump heat a large Sudbury house on its own?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the house is well insulated and the system is sized for the full load. Some owners keep a backup for the coldest days. Sudbury has 5,559 detached houses, ranking 7th of 50 for that type, so large single-family houses are the norm. We calculate the load before we quote.

faq.q: Do I need a home energy assessment?
faq.a: If the house was built before 2000, an assessment is the usual route to meeting the weatherization condition for a whole-home rebate. In Sudbury that covers most of the housing stock, since only 1,373 of 6,432 units were built from 2000 on. A newer house may skip it.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: Sudbury is 92.1% owner-occupied, with 1,671 oil homes and 3,924 on gas. Yearly servicing helps prevent many winter breakdowns, and oil systems in particular need cleaning each year.
body: ## Maintenance for a town of owners

Sudbury is 92.1% owner-occupied, so the owner is the one who deals with a failed system. Maintenance is cheaper than an emergency call, and in a large house a failure can freeze a pipe in a far corner before anyone notices.
### Oil, gas and tank gas

- **Oil (1,671 homes):** annual cleaning, nozzle and filter, combustion test.
- **Utility gas (3,924 homes):** burner, venting, controls and heat exchanger inspection.
- **Tank gas (302 homes):** the same as gas, plus a check of the supply line and regulator.
- **Heat pumps:** filters, coils, drainage and refrigerant-side checks.
### Large houses, more to look after

A big house can have more of everything: multiple zones, several thermostats, a bigger duct network and sometimes two systems. A visit covers each zone and balances airflow, since a cold bedroom is often a balancing problem.
### Seasonal timing
Book heating work in late summer or early fall. Book cooling work in spring. A house with a heat pump benefits from a check in both seasons.
### Equipment in mid-century houses

Sudbury has 1,298 homes from 1940 to 1959 and 1,910 from 1960 to 1979. Equipment in houses that old may already have been replaced once and can be near the end of a later life. A tune-up is a good time to ask how much longer a unit may last, so replacement can be planned instead of forced.

### Before you travel or close a seasonal room
In a large house it can be easy to forget a wing that nobody uses. Before a long trip, set the thermostat to a safe low temperature, ask someone to look in, and know where the main shutoff for the heating system is. A short note to us ahead of the season about the rooms that get used helps us plan the visit.
### Simple owner checks

A few owner checks help between visits. Keep outdoor units clear of leaves and snow, and if you burn oil, watch the tank gauge, since 1,671 Sudbury homes do. See the [air quality page](/cities/sudbury/indoor-air-quality) for what filters can and cannot do.

faq.q: How often should I service a Sudbury oil boiler?
faq.a: Once a year before heating season is the standard advice for oil equipment. Skipping it lets soot build up and raises the chance of a winter shutdown. In a town where oil heats 26.4% of occupied homes, 34th of 50.

faq.q: Is it worth servicing a heat pump?
faq.a: Yes. Filters and coils clog, drains block and refrigerant issues develop slowly. A yearly check keeps it running properly. Only 407 Sudbury homes heat with electricity today, so heat pumps are still a small group here, but owners who add one should include it in their yearly service plan.

faq.q: Does a house built since 2000 still need a heating tune-up?
faq.a: Yes, though the visit is shorter. Sudbury has 1,373 homes from 2000 on, 21.3% of its housing. Newer equipment still needs its safety controls, venting and burners checked each year. Houses from 1960 to 1979, the biggest age group at 1,910, may have older equipment that needs closer attention.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: Sudbury has very few old houses (6.2% from 1939 or earlier, 48th of 50) and a large middle of postwar to 1970s homes. Humidity, ventilation and filtration are the three levers, and the right mix depends on the age of the house.
body: ## Air quality in larger, mid-century and newer houses

Sudbury's houses sit in the middle of the age range: 1,298 from 1940 to 1959, 1,910 from 1960 to 1979, 1,450 from 1980 to 1999 and 1,373 from 2000 on. Only 401 date from 1939 or earlier, and 605 were built since 2010, so most of the stock sits between the very old and the very tight.
### Mid-century houses

Houses from the postwar decades through the 1970s may leak a little. Original ducts can carry years of dust, an unfinished basement can hold moisture and an addition may have its own air path. Duct cleaning makes sense after an inspection shows dirt or damage.
### Tighter newer houses
In a house built since 2010, one of Sudbury's 605 newest homes, windows and walls tend to hold air in. Cooking fumes, moisture and chemicals from furnishings linger unless ventilation moves them out.
### Humidity

- Winter air gets dry once heat is on.
- Summer basements and lower floors get damp.
- A whole-home humidifier or dehumidifier can be tied to the system.
- Keep the setting moderate so windows do not fog and mold does not grow.
### Filters
A higher-grade filter can catch finer particles, but the system has to be able to pull air through it. We check static pressure and fan capacity before suggesting a change.
### Big houses and ventilation
In a large house with several floors, air can sit still in rooms far from the return. Balancing returns, adding ventilation or a fresh-air intake can help.
### Testing
### Open space and wet ground

The town's northern half and the Hop Brook corridor hold preserved open space and wetland. Houses near wet ground can have damp cellars, so a moisture source is worth checking before buying equipment to treat the air. A dehumidifier manages the air, while a leak or drainage fault needs its own fix.

Testing gives a snapshot of humidity, carbon monoxide or particles, so fixing the source matters more than the reading. With 56.1% of Sudbury homes built before 1980, a test is a reasonable first step in an older house with a recurring complaint.

faq.q: Do I need a whole-home air cleaner in Sudbury?
faq.a: Not automatically. Start with a good filter, humidity control and ventilation. Add an air cleaner when there is a specific concern, such as allergies or smoke. In a town where 86.4% of homes are detached houses, a well-chosen filter and a ventilation fix usually cover more ground than extra equipment.

faq.q: Why does my basement smell damp?
faq.a: Moisture often comes from the ground, a leak or humid air meeting cool walls. A dehumidifier helps with the air, but the source has to be fixed. Tracing the smell comes before assuming the heating or cooling system is at fault.

faq.q: Is a newer Sudbury house a tight house?
faq.a: Often more so than an older one. Sudbury has 1,373 homes from 2000 on, including 605 built since 2010 (9.4%). Newer walls and windows tend to hold air in, so bathroom fans, range hoods and a fresh-air intake matter more. Houses from 1960 to 1979 are more likely to leak, and they are the biggest age group in town at 1,910.
